cs.t: Yes, their innovation is in hardware, not software. I also keep my 1986 HP-15C safe and use a DM15L as my everyday calculator (a new meaning for EDC...). In fact I had a NIB HP-15C LE reissue (two, in fact, but one was stolen) and resold it when I got the DM15L (and a second one for redundancy), it's a much better calculator. I have Free42 for my iPhone and iPad but I tend to use the [official HP HP-15C emulator app]( https://apps.apple.com/us/app/hp-15c-calculator/id503720774 ) instead, or PCalc.

cs.t: I have a physical HP-15C in my desk and I use the HP-15C emulator on my phone. As you can probably tell, I used that calc in college engineering classes until mine got stolen. I replaced it with an HP-28S that I used for quite a while. I bought the physical 15C a few years ago - 30 years after my original was stolen.
cs.th: Ask HN: Do you still use a hand held/desktop calculator?

cs.t: I feel the same way about not needing a physical calculator.  I have an HP-48SX and an HP-15C Collector’s Edition.  I enjoy these devices; they are high-quality and are exemplary products.  However, as a professor I have regular access to my laptop, which can run circles around my handheld calculators.  For quick calculations I open up the terminal and use the dc command, which is a command-line RPN calculator.  For more involved computations, I have Python and Common Lisp REPLs, and I also sometimes use Microsoft Excel. These days handheld calculators seem to be used the most in situations where people are restricted from using laptops and smartphones, such as during exams or in distraction-free settings.  I think the reason Texas Instruments still has a viable calculator business is because TI markets heavily in the education market.
